title: Light and optics
note: Light is an electromagnetic wave traveling at c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum and slower in matter, by the factor n. Geometric optics treats light as rays that reflect and refract (Snell's law); lenses and mirrors form images located by 1/d_o + 1/d_i = 1/f. Wave optics explains interference, diffraction, and polarization.

read.title: Rays and waves
text: Light is an electromagnetic wave: electric and magnetic fields oscillating at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel. In vacuum every such wave moves at 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. Visible light is a narrow slice of a spectrum that runs from radio waves through microwaves and infrared to ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays.

For many purposes we can treat light as rays. A ray striking a mirror reflects at the same angle it arrived. A ray crossing into a new material slows down by the factor n, the index of refraction, and bends according to Snell's law. Entering glass or water from air, it bends toward the normal. Going the other way at a steep enough angle, it cannot escape at all; this total internal reflection traps light inside optical fibers.
Lenses use refraction to form images. A converging lens can make a real image on a screen, or, with the object inside its focal length, a magnified virtual image like a magnifying glass.

Ray optics fails when light meets openings comparable to its wavelength. Then the wave nature appears: light spreads out by diffraction, and waves from two slits interfere to form bright and dark fringes. Young's double-slit experiment was early, strong evidence that light is a wave.
